blocks.heading: Carbonation
blocks.text: Carbonation begins when carbon dioxide dissolves in water, forming a weak carbonic acid. This water can react with calcium carbonate in limestone, producing soluble material that can be carried away in solution. Water entering joints helps the reaction reach the rock interior and can gradually enlarge the openings. This mechanism is chemical weathering because the material is changed through reaction and dissolution, rather than split into chemically unchanged pieces by expanding ice.

A useful sequence diagram shows rainwater acquiring carbon dioxide, the weakly acidic water entering a limestone joint, and dissolved material leaving in the water. Describe each connection: carbon dioxide makes the water weakly acidic; the water reacts with the carbonate mineral; dissolution enlarges the joint over time. Do not put oxygen in place of carbon dioxide or claim that the water must freeze. Carbonation can operate without freezing, provided the relevant water, gas and susceptible material are present. A diagram of a joint becoming wider without those details would leave the mechanism uncertain.

![Annotated carbonation sequence at a limestone joint](../../assets/images/ITEM-6137-1.2-015-INTERP-answer.png)

blocks.text: Limestone landscapes may contain solution grooves, enlarged joints, caves and other dissolution features. Formation depends on geological structure, water pathways and time; one shower does not create a large cave. Do not assume that any hole in rock proves carbonation. Identifying the rock, the chemical conditions and the removal of dissolved material makes the explanation stronger. This connects weathering to water movement and drainage. Carbonation describes a chemical process, while rivers and groundwater can transport its dissolved products; the linked sequence should not be reduced to a claim that limestone simply disappears without a mechanism.
